content: Infection in burn wounds is a critical issue as it can delay the healing process, increase the extent of scarring, and, in severe cases, lead to invasive infections that may result in patient mortality. Antibiotic prophylaxis is one of the strategies employed to prevent burn wound infections and protect patients from invasive complications. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of antibiotic prophylaxis on the rates of burn wound infections. The review included 36 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 2,117 participants. Among these, 26 trials (72%) investigated the use of topical antibiotics, seven trials assessed systemic antibiotics (four administered perioperatively and three during hospital admission or routine treatment), two trials evaluated non-absorbable antibiotics for selective decontamination of the digestive tract, and one trial examined local antibiotics delivered via the airway. A meta-analysis of 11 trials (645 participants) that studied topical prophylaxis with silver sulfadiazine revealed a statistically significant increase in burn wound infections when compared to dressings or skin substitutes (odds ratio [OR] = 1.87; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.09 to 3.19; I² = 0%). These trials were determined to have a high or unclear risk of bias. Additionally, silver sulfadiazine was associated with a significantly longer hospital stay compared to dressings or skin substitutes (mean difference [MD] = 2.11 days; 95% CI: 1.93 to 2.28). Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis in non-surgical patients was evaluated in three trials (119 participants). These studies found no evidence of a reduction in burn wound infection rates. However, one trial involving 40 participants demonstrated that systemic antibiotics (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) significantly reduced the incidence of pneumonia (risk ratio [RR] = 0.18; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.72). There was no significant effect on sepsis rates, as shown in two trials involving 59 participants (RR = 0.43; 95% CI: 0.12 to 1.61). Perioperative systemic antibiotic prophylaxis did not show any effect on the outcomes assessed in this review. Selective decontamination of the digestive tract using non-absorbable antibiotics was evaluated in two trials (140 participants). This intervention did not significantly affect the rates of infection. However, there was a statistically significant increase in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections associated with the use of non-absorbable antibiotics combined with cefotaxime compared to placebo (RR = 2.22; 95% CI: 1.21 to 4.07). Local airway antibiotic prophylaxis was assessed in one trial involving 30 participants. This study found no evidence of a difference in mortality or sepsis rates when compared to placebo. The authors concluded that the evidence regarding the effects of prophylactic antibiotics in burn patients is limited by the small number and low quality of the available studies, many of which had a high or unclear risk of bias. The most substantial evidence suggests that topical silver sulfadiazine is associated with an increased risk of burn wound infections and longer hospital stays compared to dressings or skin substitutes. However, the effects of other forms of antibiotic prophylaxis on burn wound infections remain unclear. One small study reported a reduction in pneumonia incidence with a specific systemic antibiotic regimen, but further research is needed to confirm these findings.
